newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Confusion and contradiction plague Bosnia polls.
newsitem.headline: Confusion and contradiction plague Bosnia polls.

text.p: Srebrenica is one of Bosnia's most infamous places and Srebrenik one of its more obscure, but organisers of imminent national elections got them mixed up and sent ballot forms to one that were meant for the other.

Srebrenica, the Serb-controlled town where thousands of Moslems were executed in Bosnia's worst war atrocity, received polling papers intended for Srebrenik, in Moslem-Croat federation territory, and vice-versa.
The mistake was just one episode in a saga of confusion and contradiction plaguing international preparations for Bosnia's first post-war general elections on September 14.

Problems have arisen mainly from a rush to stage the vote by a mid-September deadline written into the Dayton peace treaty, which neatly charted Bosnia's future but glossed over the determination of ethnic factions to keep old animosities alive.
Resulting inconsistencies in applying the Dayton accords have reached their peak in planning for the elections, eroding respect for the peace process.

"Dayton was so weak politically that technical disasters were bound to happen in carrying out the election," said John Fawcett of the Soros Foundation-backed International Crisis Group, a key monitoring agency.
Nationalists who sliced up Bosnia in war have been hounding moderate political rivals and doctoring voter registrations.
The Serbs have brazenly campaigned for sectarian separation in defiance of Dayton's goal of a reunified federal democracy.
But despite a host of pre-election irregularities, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) has mustered only 890 observers to watch 4,000 polling stations.
Independent monitors fear Serb authorities may "resurrect" dead people to inflate the separatist vote, since Serb forces either radically understated or did not publish war casualties.
The OSCE is doling out $5 million to political parties to help them run campaign offices and pay for advertising.
But Serb recipients are subverting Dayton's writ by touting the elections as a tool to ratify their "independence".

In a bizarre twist, $200,000 was earmarked for a party led by Zeljko Raznjatovic, a paramilitary chieftain better known as "Arkan" and named as a suspected war criminal by the U.S. government for alleged atrocities against Moslems.
The OSCE defended the donation, saying only people indicted by a U.N. war-crimes tribunal would not qualify for funding.

But the OSCE has had a tougher time explaining why it has not punished the dominant Serb nationalist SDS party for glorifying the image of "President Radovan Karadzic" despite his forced retirement from politics as a war-crimes indictee.

Analysts say the OSCE has not barred leading SDS candidates or the entire party, as it has the power to do to factions influenced by indicted war criminals or inciting defiance of Dayton, for fear the SDS might sabotage voting in its domain.
The result: the elections are safe, but without integrity, a Western humanitarian official said.

Roughly half of three million eligible voters are war refugees, the great majority barred by local ethnic powers in Bosnia from returning home in one of the gravest breaches of Dayton's letter and spirit.
But a worldwide effort to enfranchise refugees has been marred by the late or non-arrival of voting materials, including descriptions of parties and issues.
Some Moslem and Croat refugees abroad got ballot forms only in Serb Cyrillic script, and refused to vote in protest.
Bosnia's NATO-led peace force and U.N. civilian police (IPTF) have drafted plans for refugees to cross internal ethnic boundaries and vote safely in their former home towns.

But international officials say it will be mainly up to local police to secure safe passage of refugee voters, even though these police -- ill-trained and permeated by ethnic thugs -- were involved in wartime expulsions and have been instrumental in blocking repatriation of the victims.

NATO and IPTF spokesmen said on Saturday they had designated 19 crossing routes where well-armed international troops would concentrate their security presence and local police had promised to prevent anti-refugee disturbances.
Critics feel the international focus on only 19 routes and proposals to bus refugees across the lines will artificially curb free movement contrary to Dayton's provisions.
"These plans in effect discourage displaced people from using other crossing points," said Fawcett.
"This does not address the problem of lack of conditions for holding elections on this date -- a politically neutral environment and free movement -- but tries to circumvent it."
